name: milk

attributes.attribute: a central Celtic food, giving drink, butter, and cheese
protected by folklore and milking charms
a target of witch theft in Celtic belief
the abundant cow who never needed a calf and filled every vessel

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Milk was a central food of the Celtic peoples. They relied on cattle for much of what they ate, so folklore grew thick around milk. A cow after calving gave roughly a gallon to a gallon and a half of milk a day for nine months. Such a cow, called a milch cow, was a valued source of drink, butter, and cheese. In ancient Ireland these cows were so prized that they were called cumhals, and they formed the basis for valuing goods and even social rank. Irish myth told of the abundant cow, the Glas Ghaibhleann, who gave milk without ever calving and filled every vessel brought to her. When an evil person tried to milk her into a sieve, she vanished from the earth. Folklore also feared the theft of milk. Witches were said to steal milk straight from a cow's udder by passing a needle or other tool near the beast. The witch then passed the tool near her own cow, which gave forth the milk of the whole neighborhood. Her own neighbors' cows yielded only a thin fluid that would not make butter or cheese. People protected their milk with milking charms.

okr.objective: Document the role of milk in Celtic food and folklore.
